question: Which parts of the body are involved in a lower respiratory tract infection?
explanation: Think of the larynx as the dividing line! Anything below it—like the windpipe (trachea), breathing tubes (bronchi), and air sacs (alveoli)—makes up the lower respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h1)

question: Why are lower respiratory infections generally more serious than upper respiratory ones?

options.A: They cause severe localized pain in the nose.
options.B: They only happen to people with heart disease.
options.C: They directly interfere with oxygen exchange in the air sacs.
options.D: They are always completely resistant to drugs.

explanation: You've got this! When an infection hits the tiny air sacs (alveoli) deep in the lungs, it blocks oxygen from getting into the blood, making it much harder to breathe. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the most common bacteria that causes pneumonia outside of the hospital?
explanation: Also known simply as pneumococcus, this bug is the leading culprit behind everyday community-acquired pneumonia. Great to keep in mind for clinicals! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h2)

question: A patient develops a fever, cough, and shortness of breath five days after being admitted to the surgical ward for a knee replacement. How is this infection classified?
explanation: Any pneumonia symptoms appearing 48 hours or longer after a patient is admitted to a healthcare facility are classified as hospital-acquired or nosocomial pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h2)

question: What main change happens inside the tiny air sacs (alveoli) during pneumonia?

options.A: The walls permanently stretch and lose stretchiness.
options.B: Blood flow to the lungs completely stops overnight.
options.C: Fluid, pus, and cellular debris fill up the spaces.
options.D: The breathing tubes stretch out and trap air.

explanation: As the body fights the infection, fluid and white blood cells flood the alveoli. That's why air has such a hard time getting in! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h3)

question: Why does a ventilation-perfusion mismatch happen when someone has a severe lung infection?

options.A: Blocked air sacs still get blood flow, but can't get fresh air.
options.B: The throat swells up and stops breathing completely.
options.C: The heart pumps blood way too slowly for the lungs.
options.D: Mucus plugs in the windpipe block blood from reaching the heart.

explanation: Think of it as a mismatch: blood is flowing past the air sacs ready to pick up oxygen, but because they are full of fluid, there's no fresh air waiting for them. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h3)

question: When listening to the chest of a patient with lung consolidation, what sound do you usually hear?

options.B: A friction rub in the neck

explanation: You'll hear crackles (or rales)! They sound like tiny popping noises when fluid-filled air sacs suddenly snap open as the patient breathes in. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h4)

question: A patient with pneumonia says their chest hurts sharply every time they take a deep breath. What's the most likely reason?

options.A: Sudden spasms of the chest muscles
options.B: Extra pressure inside the right side of the heart
options.C: Inflamed lung linings rubbing against the chest wall
options.D: Irritation of the main breathing tubes in the throat

explanation: That sharp pain is called pleuritic chest pain. It happens when the inflamed outer lining of the lungs (pleura) rubs against the chest wall with every breath. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h4)

question: Which test is mostly used to confirm if a patient has fluid or consolidation in their lungs?
explanation: A simple chest X-ray is fast, easy, and gives a clear picture of cloudy areas or fluid buildup in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h5)

question: Why do nurses collect a sputum sample *before* starting the patient on antibiotics?

options.A: To check if the patient is allergic to drugs
options.B: To clear out the airways so they can breathe right away
options.C: To measure the red blood cell count in the airway
options.D: To find the exact germ so the right antibiotic can be given

explanation: Getting the sample first ensures the lab can grow and identify the exact bacteria without antibiotics masking the results. Smart nursing practice! [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the main medicine used to treat a confirmed bacterial lower respiratory infection?
explanation: Since it's a bacterial infection, antibiotics are needed to target and stop those specific germs from multiplying. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h6)

question: Why are bronchodilators sometimes given along with antibiotics for a lung infection?

options.A: To dry up all fluid inside the chest cavity
options.B: To bring down the patient's fever
options.C: To directly kill the bacteria in the air sacs
options.D: To relax tight airways and make breathing easier

explanation: Bronchodilators relax the muscles around the breathing tubes, opening them up so air flows more smoothly. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h6)

question: Which nursing action helps a hospitalized patient cough up thick mucus more easily?

options.A: Encouraging fluids and deep breathing exercises
options.B: Keeping the patient lying flat in bed all day
options.C: Restricting water to prevent fluid buildup in the lungs
options.D: Giving strong sleeping pills to stop the cough

explanation: Water is a natural thinner for mucus! Combined with deep breathing and controlled coughing, it helps clear the airways safely. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is your top assessment priority when caring for a patient with a severe lung infection?

options.A: Measuring the belly size every four hours
options.D: Monitoring breathing rate, depth, and oxygen levels

explanation: Respiratory status comes first! Keeping a close eye on breathing and oxygen saturation helps you catch any sudden downturn early. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h7)

question: What is an empyema?

options.A: A collapsed section of lung from mucus
options.B: A blood clot traveling from the leg to the lungs
options.C: A pocket of pus collected in the pleural space
options.D: A permanent stretching of the main breathing tubes

explanation: An empyema happens when a lung infection spreads into the space around the lungs, forming a pocket of pus that usually needs to be drained. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h8)

question: What complication happens if a localized lung infection spreads directly into the patient's bloodstream?
explanation: When germs escape the lungs and enter the general circulation, they can trigger a body-wide, dangerous inflammatory response known as sepsis. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h8)

question: Which preventive measure is especially recommended to protect older adults from bacterial pneumonia?

options.A: Taking daily antibiotics just in case

explanation: Vaccines are a powerful shield! The pneumococcal vaccine helps older adults and high-risk patients fight off dangerous strains of pneumonia. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h9)

question: Why does cigarette smoking greatly increase a person's risk of getting a lower respiratory infection?

options.A: It puts extra oxygen in the blood, which attracts germs.
options.B: It seals the air sacs shut so no air enters.
options.C: It paralyzes and destroys the tiny hairs (cilia) that sweep dirt out of the airways.
options.D: It stops the stomach from making acid.

explanation: Smoke damages the cilia—the microscopic brooms of the respiratory tract. Without them working, mucus and germs get trapped in the lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T6#GNS213_U2_T6_h9)
